review:
TLDR: If you enjoyed Divinity or any of the other games like it, this is a home run and despite some changes to the mechanics, manages to be a bright, shining light among the crowd.

After thoroughly enjoying the first Divinity game as a two-player experience at home, it was time to expand things online with all my friends. Larian Studios have really shined with Divinity and it continues with Divinity II, which is pretty much bigger and better in about ever sense of the word - and not just in size, but in quality. And while some of the changes may not necessarily be for the better - nothing was broken along the way and the scope of the story, characters and the world has been greatly expanded making up for any questionable mechanics in my eyes.

Looks and Stuff: It's not that the first game looked bad - it was just a bit rough around the edges. Divinity II smooths all those edges out and presents a truly and fully fleshed-out game, both in environments, enemies and characters. But the visuals aren't the only thing improved, with a truly impressive vocal cast and a sweeping score to go along with the action. If you want an immersive experience, this is the perfect game to get lost in - even moreso than something like Witcher 3 or Skyrim - and that in of itself is an impressive result.

Story: Epic in every sense of the world - the game takes place in the same world, Rivellon, as the first, but we fast forward quite a bit. In this future time, our Divine Order finds itself rather adrift after the death of Lucian the Divine (kind of like the pope - but with more direct contact with the gods) and the rather underwhelming replacement who is trying to hold things together. To make matters worse, it seems that people who can harness Source (aka magic) are suddenly attracting creatures known as Voidwoken - who tend to kill everyone in sight when they appear. Thus sourcerers of all stripes are being rounded up and taken to Fort Joy (aka magic prison island), fitted with source-cancelling collars and kept under a tight watch by the Magisters. The rather robust introduction lets you take on the role of one of the six origin characters (each with their own in-depth story) or you can create your own from a variety of options including races and whether or not you want to be undead or not. Then it throws you on a ship bound for Fort Joy and lets you explore the myriad mechanics of the game you will be spending the better part of a year playing.

Fort Joy itself is really just an extension of the introduction - and it can be a bit overwhelming at first to realize this huge starting area is just a really long tutorial. You soon learn that your (chosen) characters is one of a handful of Godwoken - that is, an analog to one of the gods in the Rivellon pantheon and can ascend to the Divine if they so choose. Of course, this means escaping Fort Joy, figuring out the issue with the Voidwoken, confronting the current Divine Order and all manner of side quests along the way. In addition, the six origin characters each have their own stories - from dealing with a demonic entity in their head to confronting many shadows of their past - and while you don't have to play as each of the characters to explore their stories (single player can control up to four - if they don't royally piss them off), it provides plenty of incentive for replay.

Gameplay: As in the first game, the large world is presented in a top-down perspective with the ability to wander as you will - talk to every person (and animal, if you have the right perk), take everything in sight (though stealing will get you in trouble) and kill anyone you feel like. Many characters will give you various side-quests and it is advisable to do as many as you can because, as in the first game, enemies are finite and if you will need every drop of XP you can get to improve your stats or you can get in a pickle with later battles. Speaking of stats, you have many - base stats like strength (tank's favorite), finesse (archer's delight), constitution (hp for the win) intelligence (better magics), memory (learn more skills across the board) and wits (spotting secrets, going first in battle and hitting harder). You can also choose from a wide variety of preset classes that let you really dig deep into how you want to play the game. On top of that, civic points let you be a thief, a persuasion machine or identify items. Usually you want to focus on just a couple of these for the best results. Finally you have the rarer talents - including the likes of Pet Pal (talk to animals), Opportunist (attacks of opportunity) and Leech (heal while standing in blood). Talents can both affect combat and the game in general and offer a wide array of combinations to try out.

If you played the first game, combat is going to feel a lot different this time around. That is because the game has decided Physical and Magic armor are now separate things - you have to whittle one or the other down (using physical or magical attacks) before actually doing any real damage. In addition until that bar is consumed, your physical and magic abilities will also not take affect (thus things like knockdown or elemental affects are null and voided). This mechanic does take getting used to and it also seems to nerf some of the best attacks from the first game. Likewise, your own character has their own bar based on the equipment they have on and often you must balance things out because going full physical or magic is recipe for disaster in the long run. That also means your character builds must be taken into account as you must strike a balance with magic, unfortunately, proving somewhat underwhelming compared to a full-on physical assault.

Replay value: Off the charts, provided you want to sink several hundred hours into this world more than once.

Presentation: 5/5
Story: 5/5
Gameplay: 4/5
Replay: 5/5
Overall (not an average): 4.5/5

review:
This is a game I thought I was going to love, but honestly, I think it is pure garbage. After 6 hours, I've already dropped it after reading that it won't really get any better after Fort Joy. I know I've played it for a very short time, but I can't take it anymore.

1. The tone is super weird for an RPG - quirky, sarcastic, and humorous while trying to have a serious background. It wouldn't be a problem if these quirks were sporadic, but almost every character talks like they were written by a stupid Millennial. It makes me not want to take the story seriously AT ALL, and a compelling story and world are what make me want to keep playing an RPG. What are the stakes? What happens if I fail? What happens if I succeed? Do I care if everyone in this world dies or not? This is a rare breed of game where I don't even care about causing havoc because I think the setting itself is dull.

2. It is a game with tons of (usually pointless) dialogue, but once I realized that the walls of text are just white noise, I stopped caring. In games like Mass Effect and New Vegas, for instance, what you say actually makes a difference, and you can avoid combat or provoke mass killings based solely on what you choose and your roleplaying, which seems to be the total opposite in Original Sin 2, where you'll always be dragged to a combat situation, whether you like it or not.

3. Despite being the most praised aspect of the game, the combat is boring as all hell, and this comes from a guy who enjoys turn-based combat. The system fails to explain how to properly engage in its mechanics, so you'll have to do a lot of trial-and-error and look it up online to learn how to properly play the damn thing. I am not the type of guy who'll invest my time trying to understand a complex game that I don't care about.

Overall, I think this is either a) an extremely overrated game, or b) a product that's designed for someone radically different than me. Either way, I don't think it is a compelling game, and definitely not worth the money.

You practically have to go in already knowing what build and how your going to build into it before you even start playing. In my play through with friends, what I found is that splitting my points between both strength and int it caused me to be wildly under powered by fairly early act 2 and I quickly had to full path on int with enough strength to have good armor and unless I was gonna start going range I had to dump dual wield for two hand staff as only wands and staffs use int and staffs are the only melee int, while finesse has knives and javelins alongside bows and strength only has melee weapons where in DnD there are strength range and magic based melee and maybe maces, as a cleric’s iconic weapon is a mace, or a rapier could have been an answer for one handed int melee. Here me and one of my friends are dying as due to me dual wielding swords and him wanting to go full summoner meanwhile our other friend who went archer was killing guys in single turns. The summoner had to go wand and shield to survive and we found summoner isn’t that great later in the game as it kinda falls off, but theirs no way, besides selling random stuff or just stealing everything, to get back that money spent on those books and I really don’t want to play the STUPID STEAL EVERYTHING META. Add a point system that allows you to chose what skills you want, have memory be a cost per spell it’d be same thing anyways. review:
- Note: While I do recommend this game, there are many caveats.

- Pros: In my 34hrs that was basically only Act 1, was I slow per say? yes to an extent, however there is plenty of content on the starting Act to fill that time.

The characters are very interesting and the story is as well, far superior to BG3 in many ways regarding the player character and the intrigue of your companions as well as content you interact with.

The gear and "classes" in this game are very fun, but it will take a ton of trial and error to figure out the "optimal" way to go about your class, the combat is VERY different from BG3 and being able to just bonk really hard usually won't work.

- Cons: This game is really hard. Even on classic you will die ALOT. Trust me, do not rush, level up as much as possible, steal what you can (I didn't do that) and do as much side content as possible to level. SKILL BOOKS are EVERYTHING! Read them, buy them or steal them, you won't get skills/abilities from leveling up, they come from scrolls, books, items. While this makes the game more interesting, it also makes it super hard or a slog most of the time, if you thought the long fights in BG3 were bad, these are worse.

QoL Markers. The quests in the game don't really explain anything, you have to pay attention to what NPCs are saying and godforbid you look away or get side tracked and don't remember, you will wander for a long time around the quest markers that don't elaborate.

Overall it was good, of course it was. But, some personal grudges: 

I much preferred the beginning of this game to the end. The end felt rushed and some story lines poorly written. I understand that this was one of the things they tried to correct with the definitive edition, so I imagine it was even more rushed before. I feel like the character’s perspectives on certain plot points change too unexpectedly. For example, the game goes from people not even knowing of the God King’s existence, to assuming its common knowledge. Other smaller plot points are done very oddly as well, and I feel like the game significantly falls off in writing quality in the final Act. It doesn’t take away from the overall lore, which is great, just some of the late game writing around things was poor. 

The whole gimmick of using source as a recourse to cast spells and abilities, was really just a way to waste time. Because in each act you can set up teleporter Pyramids where there is a source fountain, and have max Source for each fight. It just means a 2 minute excursion after every fight fidgeting around the source fountain, trying to get all my characters in the right place. 

Only being allowed to take 4 characters with you off Fort Joy is a cheap way to increase replayability. 

Some of the Level design, all throughout the game, was odd. I was rarely level matched with enemies. Either over or under levelled. There was certainly a place I could go to and where the enemies would be appropriately levelled, but I don’t know which direction I should go in for the optimal level matched route. I just went wherever felt most natural, which for me meant being underlevelled at the beginning of every act and overlevelled at the end. Except for the final act where I never got the level 20, despite doing every quest available. Which is odd because at times the game seems to presume that most players will only see one part of the game, and move on. That the average player will not try to see everything before moving on, but only do the things necessary to progress. In Fort Joy for example, even if you’ve already found an exit, you can still talk to people and ask them if they know a way out. In Reaper’s Coast, once you’ve got the 3 source points, you don’t get much from pursuing the other people, and the dialogue around that seems underdeveloped even. Which is strange considering it seems like you do need to do almost everything to be appropriately leveled. Also why wouldn’t you want to do as much as you can anyway? 

I felt like half way through the game I had basically every spell unlocked. 

It’s too easy to accidentally do the wrong thing in combat. 

Inventory management is a joke. 

Despite everything, it’s still very good.

review:
BG3 converted me to CRPGs so I wanted to go back and try DOS2. I really enjoyed it and will definitely play again to try out different story/companion outcomes which I think speaks well of it as a game nearly a decade old.  As I expected the companion characters and story choices are engaging, complex and sometimes tricky to navigate, just as i hoped for.  I found I didn't connect on an emotional level quite as much - I suspect that's down to the lack of cinematics/animated cutscenes.  That's not a criticism of this game - it's just a reflection of the age & budget - but it's something to be aware of if you're thinking of picking it up in 2026, it's not going to look/feel like BG3.  But i still loved the art style and the writing and I can't wait to see what Larian will be able to create for Divinity.

I found the different skills/combat system to have both pros & cons compared to BG3s adaptation of 5E.  The freedom of a classless system is really fun and I found that I preferred an AP/cooldown system, rather than having spell slots and Actions/Bonus Actions - it made me think differently about how I built my party and approached combat.  I'm in the minority that likes the Physical/Magical Armour system, I think it adds something to have to plan around that.  
What I was less keen on was the buying skillbooks and the memory points system.  Having to traipse around vendors trying to find the skillbook I'd decided I wanted felt like a chore and the memory point system felt a bit too restrictive.  I felt like if the selling point is flexibility it should be easier to just try things out - not a complete free-for-all but a bit less restriction on where you can pick up skills and how many you can have equipped.  I also wasn't a huge fan of the way initiative works (although I'm still not sure I properly understand how initiative works).  The combat in this game is not easy, even on Balanced, and it can get pretty demoralising to sit there while a dozen enemies set your whole party (and most of the surrounding scenery) on fire, killing 3 of them, meaning the 4th spends their turn resurrecting people/trying to not be on fire.  I'd prefer having more scope to use character builds/abilities/equipment to manipulate turn order or action economy so I could make that happen less.

Overall though I really loved the game and I'm looking forward to getting better at it :)

review:
What to say about Divinity: Original Sin 2?

Coming off of Baldur's Gate 3 and into this was a trip. There are obvious differences, a lack of cut scenes and RNG in character check based moments - ex. I am not rolling a die to see if I pass a persuasion check.

And there is of course combat, which is based on an action point system, and rather than phases of combat is more focused on the power you build as well as elemental synergies.

But what probably is its largest difference, and the difference that is most subtle in first impressions, is the world building and storytelling.

DOS2 is more intrigued in its subtlety when telling its story. With a lack of cut scenes and comparatively a more broad “chosen one” fable, it’s more about piecing together the atrocities and happenings across its four acts. Opting many times for combat, which is a storytelling mechanic in of itself as the game loads you and your party slowly with power to overcome it's largest obstacles, and in turn deliver its universe.

It’s in this overall hunt for power, mixed with the brilliant yet simple combat system, that makes this game standout above Baldur’s Gate 3 for me.

Don’t get me wrong, I think BG3 is a better title objectively. I would recommend it to anyone, and I truly think it is a game everyone should play at least once.

But through meticulous game design - this idea of presenting an adversary that is impossible to overcome until an eventual wallop hours later - while growing synergies and strength through your team as you rise to becoming a God, is an addicting loop.

I think BG3 does this amazing thing where there's always a solution, and that doesn't always mean combat. This is the bread and butter of Dungeons & Dragons: you and your party finding unique solutions to things that can't be solved with violence, or even don't want to solve with violence. Its story is riddled with this philosophy.
And in turn, it becomes sequential. You're always moving forward.

DOS2 is not this. DOS2 is combat and patience. It's you overcoming and growing outwards, not so much inwards. It's what some would call a PowerRPG. 

There are some solutions that can be passed by a Persuasion check, but even then I found myself forced into a situation that felt demanding of bloodshed.

But this works for its story, you are on your way to becoming Divine. You are gaining power, literally bit by bit, until one day the enemies of titan size become bugs under your shoe. The game's first act of Fort Joy is textbook of this philosophy. You begin completely starved of your tiny amount power, and in your escape you are able to crush all that held you captive.

It’s through these moments, while building a relationship of action through your party and NPCs, that allows these story beats to rise high.

There were many moments in my 90+ hour run that made my jaw drop. That sucked the air from my lungs as NPC party members made choices, as I was forced to choose the best of two terrible options, as twists to my own destiny came to light causing me to rethink my entire adventure.

And when these two things came together - genius combat and beautiful storytelling - you get one of the greatest experiences possible.

I am heartbroken that this adventure is over.

There are not many games that I can happily say I’d keep playing. Hell, I tout and support shorter games, or moreso games that know when to get out.
I love Resident Evil, specifically 2, but I don’t think that game needs another hour, nor would I want one. I loved Oblivion but by hour 40 I was ready to call it and move on. Same with Hollow Knight. Or Dark Souls at 50-60 hours. And there’s even instances, like me playing The Witcher 3, where I did put in the 80+ hours, but to do so sometimes felt like I had to force myself to boot up and get into it.

Never once did I feel this way with Divinity 2. I could have gone on for another 90, truly.

This is not a normal occurrence in the slightest for me.

What’s funny is my friend and I tried to play DOS2 after beating BG3 last year and after 5 hours were so thrown off by the how different the combat, dialogue, and character checks were (played what I think was a week after 80+ hours in BG3, too soon) that we didn’t return.

But upon my solo return, I fell hard.

And even with BG3, which again I do think is objectively a better game, I never felt like I could continue forever. And maybe that’s just because I was in a party with 3 players and not solo and it was such a thing to get us all on at the same time that even finishing was a miracle.

But I could play Divinity: Original Sin 2 forever.

It has quickly become a Top 5 - if not more than likely my favorite game of all time.

<3

Masterwork.

review:
The game is pretty great. It does a couple things I super hate, but mostly, it's an exemplar of the cRPG genre. The combat is unassailably good, though it is pretty unforgiving. You get enough abilities that combat never feels stale and the enemies are at least as well equipped and skilled as your party. 

The roleplay parts are fine. It's cool you can play a prebuilt character or roll your own and if you roll your own, the characters you aren't playing are you companions. The writing is pretty good and the tone is FAR more consistent than the first game, which felt like a Discworld novel, but in a bad way.

The negatives are largely how out-of-combat healing works. You can and probably will have a character die from a residual effect immediately after a combat encounter because you couldn't hit Rest or case a healing spell fast enough. Then you have to burn a resurrection scroll, which are expense and rare.

The game is also super stingy with loot. This isn't a bad thing, but if you're coming from Dragon Age or Pillars of Eternity or even the first Divinity Original Sin, but it is something to be aware of. Your party will be only half equipped for a while.

Overall, it's a great game.

review:
Gameplay: 8
Combat very similar to the Original Sin 1, but more balanced, without overpowered spells that could one shot bosses in the first game, and with way less randomness. For the latter is responsible quite unique system of physical and magical armor, that works as the second health and must be depleted to apply a debuff. But once depleted - all the debuffs goes with 100% chance. But that is still a Larian game, so sometimes systems works not so reliable, which generate a weird wonky impression from combat in some fights. 

And because it is an Original Sin game, the whole screen will be covered with fire, blood, ice, smoke and all the versions of them every single fight. I really hope that in the upcoming new Divinity game that mess of elements will be not so messy.

Visuals: 9
Did I mention the messiness of the combat? It is never a bad thing to mention it again - so messy it is. But outside of the millions of elemental effects covering the screen every fight and overcluttered inventory, all the rest visual parts of the game are very good. Landscapes, scenery, attempts in cutscenes from time to time, design of enemies and factions, everything done nicely. The game only lacks of proper cinematic close-up cutscenes, but that is only because of the budged, judging by the studios next game.

Sound: 10
One thing that is stand out is the music. It is absolutely amazing and giving a proper mood for various scenes in the game. The idea of creating a theme for the whole soundtrack and then using in many variations is just brilliant. I got same feeling during BG3 playthrough, but seems like Larian came to this idea with Original Sin 2, way before Baldur's Gate 3.

Voiceover is also on a very high level. Especially the animal characters. In general speaking with animals is like a separate and very fun layer of the game, filled with jokes, clues and references.

Story: 8
The story is way more serious than in the first Original Sin, and more often than not the game is filled with thinking and investigation, than joking and goofing around. But despite the looming apocalypse and all the corpses and blood covering most of the locations, the game's atmosphere doesn't feel dark or dramatic. Because the devs in their wisdom made everything colourful, filled the world with some funny objects and comical characters, and of course too pathos and comically evil enemies. "Never-ever" phase will haunt me from time to time though.

The plot itself is quite interesting and intriguing, but the lack of memorable characters and surprisingly a lack of choices in any crucial moment prevent the story from being really good. Also it is beyond me why the companions are never participate in conversations. Sure, there are few dialogs for each companion, but they are forcing player to fully switch to that character and often happens even without opportunity to listen to them.

Personal rate: 8.5/10
More than a successful sequel to Divinity: Original Sin, where the devs fixed a lot of problems of the first game, but also didn't forget to bring new ones! Yes the game is still quite messy in many ways, same as the original. But this time it is way more polished experience with more comprehensive storytelling and an intriguing plot. 

Especially funny to play DOS2 after experiencing the first DOS and Baldur's Gate 3, because that way it is surprising how much more polished the game in comparison with DOS1 and how close it is to BG3. Pretty much BG3 without huge budged for cutscenes and party dialogs, but with combat system from Original Sin 1.

Eventually it is a very strange but definitely enjoyable cocktail of an RPG. Now I can see why Baldur's Gate 3 development was given to Larian Studios and not to InXile or Obsidian. Definitely was a good choice.

review:
it is a mid game that is rightfully praised for its combat interactivity, talking with pets, and providing players with cheap skinner box - dopamine rush when following the game design and looting every crate or barrel.

Why I don't like it,
You liberate Fort Joy, killing every magister, and no one cares. Not even a simple line of acknowledgment. And this isn't like a murderous psychopath path, this is the path the game pushes you to.

Scripted events prevent you from saving unimportant NPCs, no matter what you do, The game wants them to die and there's nothing you can do about it. The game will try to trick you into believing you have the ability to save them. You don't. Everything is scripted.

They introduce a companion by having that companion threaten to kill you, forcing you to metagame to justify sparing that idiotic companion. In addition, that companion's quest is broken if you don't allow the companion to murder a lizard, forcing you to choose between blocking access to content or immersing yourself.

Options to express yourself through dialogue are lacking and overly buffoonish. The stoic options are gone, and what you are left with are lines that would feel at home in a parody movie.

Most positive reviews are from people who never actually finished the game. Without 50%-70% of game time will be spent on leveling, looting and shopping and not on doing anything fun.  (Owlcat games also suffer from this specific issue.) 

Combat is a huge major downgrade from Original Sin 1. Creativity and battle mages are punished. You are guided to min max and to push yourself to deal either all magic damage or physical damage.  Once the enemy's armor shatters  you can keep them perma-stunlocked.  Before their armor shatters nerfing and effects do nothing. And if you already broke their armor you might aswell finish them. Leaving you with aoe and direct damage focused skills. 

The game forces you to be a people pleaser, Roleplaying = Agreeing.
If you challenge a companion’s flawed logic, you’re punished.
If you try to set boundaries, you’re punished.
If you act like a rational person who doesn't want to be involved in "comical" nonsense, you’re punished.

The game is a one big skinner box looting simulator while telling you all the while that you are the chosen one. While many like grinding and looting boxes for half the game, I don't. 

The game shines when you talk with animals, because that is the only time the writing style fits the narrative. In other times the writing feels like AI, wordy overly flowery and a lot of telling rather than showing.

review:
The jankiest game I've ever played, literally every single part of the game is fighting you when you play it. Every single system has pushback, this game could use a ton of QoL  features, its really not a surprise that BG3 was a huge hit while this was niche.

Camera: horrible, pixel hunting, zoomed out, you literally cannot see loot without holding alt, Player movement: you cannot see a ton of areas, where you need to go, where is walkable, is that ladder approachable? Click to move also feels really detached and lifeless, your party members will also refuse to move through anything remotely harmful, even If I can just use a bedroll to heal, hope you like swapping party members 4 times for a puddle of poison! It feels like just moving through the world is annoying.

Character builds and stats: Hope you like Youtube tutorials, because nothing is adequately explained, the initial character creator is a nightmare. Every single physical damage build should level warfare, there are a ton of one point wonders and overall its just unintuitive and confusing. You know in Souls most things work, you just figure out what the scaling is and then upgrade it, this is the OPPOSITE system, where most things don't work unless you have a deep understanding of when to break rules.
Examples: Two handed weapon users > Warfare, Bow users > Warfare, Daggers? Again, use warfare. Spells work against each other (fire and water), some parties are terrible because they split what armor they focus on.

Combat: CC everything at all costs forever, anything else is almost objectively incorrect, also its a pixel hunting nightmare of various particle effects, hope you enjoy rotating the camera, double checking everything and never misclick one mm away from a character because now your mage is about to give their highly armored warrior a hug. The armor system also sucks, as it forces you to pick a lane, or risk taking longer to CC something, which is ALWAYS what you want to do.

Story: Extremely slow and generic at the same time, its not that hard to understand but nothing really happens, it feels like a tv series where the main plot surfaces now and then but its mostly little mini adventures. The dialogue varies but overall is engaging and well made. I've played 11 hours and the story has been barebones.

Inventory management: Holy hell this sucks, its just a massive grid, sure you can filter by items, but most items are useless and serve no purpose, shells, pots, intestines etc, its just clutter for clutters sake, and there is also crafting, so you pick up what looks like common useful items just to find your bags filled with garbage, also everyone has their own storage, so you have to share potions, share gold if one is better at bartering etc, it just takes a simple system and makes it a chore.

Markets/bartering: Every single character has an inventory, can be bartered with, and will trade based on their attitude towards you, so enjoy speaking with everyone in case they have a cool skill book, what a tedious horrible waste of time.

Equipment: Feels like nothing is unique, its just raw stat checks, more similar to Diablo or an ARPG, did you get some cool, unique quest reward? Well a basic ass item has higher number, so swap it, really takes away from the game because most gear is painfully generic.

Dialog: Honestly the best part of the game, but it also suffers from far too many edgy characters and generic templates. Red prince seems to be a favorite because of how unique he is, shame most other characters aren't. Lots of tonal wiplash, with dialog choices that are extremely out of place, and NPCs barely react to the edgy options, if you are going to have completely offbeat choices, I expect relative reactions.

The game also treats violence as inconsequential, it loses its bite very quickly, people get killed frequently for next to nothing, so you stop caring, there is no build up, stakes or anything, fights to the death are just what happens when you insult someone I suppose.

Overall I felt this game was made to be bragged about, not actually played, it's pure friction zero flow, I could never just relax and explore, lose myself in the world, the game would often an jarringly remind me THIS IS A VIDEOGAME, SORT YOUR INVENTORY, TALK TO EVERYONE, YOU MISSED THE CAVE, sometimes you need narrow your scope and think about the player journey, instead of "look at all our mechanics, sure they don't mesh and the UI sucks, but its a lot right?

The games biggest failing is just playing it feels mildly annoying, like work, like I'm enduring something instead of discovering, waiting for a carrot that will never arrive. Let it stay in the history books, a janky precursor story instead of a game you should actively look to enjoy.

review:
Positives:
1. Classless character creation. It's not like BG3 where you're placed on a set, specific upgrade path based on your class. If you want to play a scoundrel without backlash or adrenaline, go right ahead. Do you want to play a necromancer/pyro/scoundrel character? Cool. You can do that.

2. Progression is not locked to level-ups. Leveling up is fun, but you get new skills by buying skill books from traders. This means you aren't desperately waiting to level up to get cool new features to play around with.

3. The combat depth is incredible. The game encourages you to play around your environment. High ground gives you bonus range and damage on ranged skills. Barrels can be broken to spread surfaces like poison, fire, and oil. Surfaces can be blessed to turn negative terrain effects like fire into sources of healing and buffs. Surfaces can be cursed to turn neutral terrain into dangerous terrain and dangerous terrain into even worse terrain. Some surfaces can even be mixed to create new surfaces like electrified steam and frozen blood.

4. The arena. I, too, have had my attention span dangerously eroded by the attention economy, and the ability to load up arena mode, pick some premade characters, and just fight a few matches is just the right amount of instant gratification for me.

Negatives:
1. Stunlocks. This game features lots and lots and lots of stunlocks. You can do it to your enemies and they can do it to you. Stuns in this game are resisted by armor, meaning once a character's armor is broken, stuns become guaranteed. This means that once your physical armor is broken you can expect to be knocked down 4 turns in a row and once your magic armor is broken you can expected to be frozen and shocked until you die.

2. The graphics. They did not age well.

3. The initiative order. The initiative is rigged. The game is specifically programmed to play in a specific order: Player turn, enemy turn, player turn, enemy turn. If you kill an enemy, the game will move slower enemies higher in the turn order to fill the gap left by the dead enemy. This means that targeting characters who are higher in the turn order to finish them off before they get a chance to attack, which is a critical strategy in many other turn-based RPGs, just doesn't work in this one. It also means that boosting your initiative in this game is pretty much pointless, since an enemy with +1 initiative can always go before your second fastest character, even if their initiative bonus is +7.


I'm sure there's more I'm missing, but this game is a ton of fun, so instead of finishing this review, I'm just going to go load up another arena match and play that instead.

Played on Tactician, completionist run.

+ Act 1 and Act 2 are masterpieces of CRPG design — 10/10.
+ The combat system is innovative, strategic, and extremely fun.
+ The OST is great, the voice acting is strong, and the writing in the first half is mostly excellent.

- Act 3 is mid. There’s too much repetition, and burnout begins to creep in. 
- Act 4 / Arx is the worst-designed “big city” I’ve ever seen in a CRPG. It doesn’t feel lived in. It doesn’t feel like a capital. It feels like a cardboard container where the developers stuffed every remaining boss to clean up unresolved questlines. There’s no sense of civilian life. No organic exploration. The city doesn’t even have a tavern — not even the suggestion that one existed before the siege.
- Itemization goes from interesting and build-defining to borderline nonsensical in the endgame.

It honestly feels like Larian split their effort between Acts 3 and 4 when they should have focused on making one strong, cohesive final act. I hate when a game I genuinely love collapses in its second half. It sours the entire experience.

This game has some of the best roleplaying potential as well as some of the most engaging turn-based combat I've ever seen in a game of its ilk. Each monster you fight feels unique and has its own special skillset that makes the world feel unpredictable and dangerous, even on relatively low difficulty.

The lore, the characters, the worldbuilding, everything is fleshed out and feels alive, engaging, and lived-in. You can interact with pretty much everything and everyone, and the game will acknowledge all of your choices from the smallest act of kindness to the most egregious act of selfishness; it won't treat you like a hero or a villain for doing any specific act, just show you the fruits of your actions and what they result in.

The combat is genuinely engaging and makes you feel the peril of danger. It is brutal but fair, and you will realize that in the majority of cases your loses will be the result of your own carelessness or lack of strategic planning. Even a relatively trivial encounter can be deadly if you get sloppy. You can play on insane difficulty honor-mode if you love the challenge or on story mode if you just want to roleplay and focus on interaction with the other characters, building your party however you like.

If you like turn-based combat games, a good story where choices matter, and characters with complex personalities, then this is a very good title; it's probably not a perfect fit for everyone but I'd say at least give it a try.

8/10

review:
Divinity: Original Sin 2: A Masterclass in RPG Excellence
In an era where role-playing games often streamline complexity for accessibility, Larian Studios delivered something extraordinary with Divinity: Original Sin 2—a game that dares to offer both depth and approachability, and succeeds brilliantly at both.

Freedom Redefined
What sets DOS2 apart is its astonishing commitment to player agency. This isn't a game that pays lip service to choice; it genuinely respects your decisions. Want to solve a quest through diplomacy? Combat? Stealth? Outright murder of everyone involved? The game accommodates all approaches with remarkable grace. The emergent gameplay possibilities feel genuinely limitless—environmental interactions allow you to freeze water, electrify puddles, teleport enemies into chasms, or combine elements in ways the developers probably never anticipated. Every encounter becomes a creative playground.

Characters That Breathe
The Origin Character system represents narrative design at its finest. Each pre-made companion—from the sardonic undead Fane to the righteous Ifan ben-Mezd—arrives with rich backstories, personal quests, and genuinely compelling arcs. They feel like protagonists of their own stories, whether you choose to play as them or recruit them to your party. The voice acting brings these characters to vivid life, and the writing avoids fantasy clichés in favor of nuanced, morally complex storytelling.

Tactical Combat Perfection
The turn-based combat system is nothing short of exceptional. Built on an AP (Action Point) system that rewards strategic thinking, every battle demands careful consideration of positioning, environmental hazards, and ability synergies. The elemental interaction system—where fire and poison create explosive combinations, water conducts electricity, and blood can be frozen or electrified—transforms combat into elaborate tactical puzzles. Fights feel consequential, challenging, and endlessly satisfying to master.

A World Worth Exploring
Rivellon is a setting crafted with meticulous care. From the prison island of Fort Joy to the haunting streets of Arx, each location tells stories through environmental detail, hidden secrets, and memorable encounters. The world responds to your actions and racial choices—playing as an undead means concealing your identity, while Lizards and Elves face distinct social dynamics. This reactivity makes exploration feel purposeful and rewarding.

Cooperative Excellence
The four-player co-op implementation is revelatory. DOS2 doesn't just allow multiplayer—it's designed around it, with systems for party disagreements, split decision-making, and collaborative problem-solving. Friends can pursue different objectives simultaneously, debate moral choices through the game's dialogue system, or combine their abilities in combat for devastating combos. It's the rare RPG that feels equally magnificent solo or with companions.

A Soundtrack for the Ages
Borislav Slavov's score deserves special mention. From the hauntingly beautiful main theme to the atmospheric exploration music and pulse-pounding battle tracks, the soundtrack elevates every moment. It's music that stays with you long after you've stopped playing.

Endless Replayability
With multiple origin stories, countless build possibilities across deep character customization, branching narratives, and a robust Game Master mode that allows players to create their own campaigns, DOS2 offers potentially hundreds of hours of content. Each playthrough reveals new interactions, hidden consequences, and alternative solutions you never discovered before.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 isn't just an outstanding RPG—it's a benchmark against which other games in the genre must be measured. It proves that depth and accessibility aren't mutually exclusive, that player freedom can coexist with strong narrative design, and that turn-based combat can be every bit as thrilling as real-time action. Larian Studios didn't just create a great game; they crafted a modern masterpiece that respects player intelligence, rewards creativity, and delivers an unforgettable journey through one of the most richly realized fantasy worlds in gaming.

For anyone who loves role-playing games, Divinity: Original Sin 2 isn't just recommended—it's essential.

review:
After restarting the game 5 times I decided on installing mods so I can use all six characters in one play through. I wouldn't recommend it because the story feels bloated because of the number of storylines that are very loosely related to one another. I would recommend playing with only one other character on your team (going through the story 6 times). It'll give you a faster paced story with less running around for not much reward. Playing with mods (level 30, best gear, easiest difficulty, and all six companions at once) took me about 40 hours, which could have been cut down to about 25 hours if I didn't wander around aimlessly all the time (I was expecting something to happen or one of the characters to actually say something interesting).

The high point of the game is Fort Joy. The story goes down hill form there. The "God King" never shows up in person, making him a poor antagonist. Lucian only shows up at the end where he tells you to die. Dallis, turns out to be an impersonator who ate the original Dallis, and is Fane's daughter (which felt not only unnecessarily tacked on, but also fairly mean spirited). She only shows up three times before the final battle like a mustache twirling villain. I guess the real villain of the story is Braccus Rex who's artifacts and presence is seen throughout the game and is the link to all the other antagonists in the game? 

The main character I choose was Lohse, who is frankly the best written of them bunch, which isn't saying much since there isn't much actual story in this game (more so it's written as one plot following another/ "and then this happened and then that happened, etc." (I have no idea what happened to Jahan the demon hunter after getting to Arx, he just disappeared and no one mentions him after that). Ifan's story got cut short due to Sebille killing the guy at the sawmill before I could ask him questions. Beast was always acting shy and only acts up twice in Ripper Bay (when I attempted to kill the dwarf gang leader and when I ate the two dwarf spirits in graveyard) and his journal entry never updated when I killed the queen and everyone around her when I first encountered them in the sewers. I didn't talk to Fane, his journal entry never changed from his initial Fort Joy entry to get a skin mask from a guy I had already killed, The Red Prince just kept asking for his wife so I just never interacted with him.

For whatever reason, after soloing the entirety of Fort Joy and then going on to recruit all the other characters Ifan was minus 35 attitude, while everyone else was plus 25 attitude. I had to use a mod to get everyone up to plus 100. 
All the source masters (except Jahan) are bad guys and you shouldn't feel bad about taking them out. They are either demons or cause void woken to wreak the Ripper Coast. 

If you are playing a custom character I would recommend only enlisting Ifan and Lohse. Sebille's story is basically done by the after the saw mill and the Shadow Prince's note says he basically doesn't care if Sabille kills him as long as he manages to kill the elf tree, which Sebille herself doesn't even care about, the Red Prince is only concerned in chasing after his princess, Beast has a boring plot with tedious quests, and Fane is just hounded by void woken that tell him to change sides every time they see him, 

What I don't like was the seemingly random and forced sexual encounters that always came out of nowhere, to the point that every time I asked any of my companions a question it would devolve into some sexual nonsense. Somehow Sebille became my romantic interest, even though I never spoke to her. I only gave her body parts to consume and didn't even kill the elf tree (I killed Saheila automatically when playing Lohse in Fort Joy and I ate the Shadow Prince before killing all the elves on the nameless isle before they could talk to me so I couldn't kill the elf tree myself). Why don't I have a choice to refuse?

The gay stuff in the this game is often subtle/random and frankly nonsensical considering the setting. In the last area of the game (Arx) you'll see the White Blonde haired male villain (Linder Kemm) getting ready to kill the female brown skinned lesbian whose "wife" is yelling for someone save my wife from execution (lol). Since I was playing Ifan, I decided to role play a Islamic "Paladin" for 10 seconds and killed everyone there. Thus saving the city from the woke mind virus. The lesbian is also revealed to have been in another evil faction so I was correct in my decision. As the game goes on you will also notice an increase in non White characters, form nearly zero in Fort Joy to a Black woman with a giant mohawk casually waking around in Arx after you've cleared the place of enemies.

It feels like there aren't any countries/governing bodies in the game? It's like 3 or 4 gangs running around killing people and doing whatever they wanted, but I didn't see a local mayor or baron that stood out, it was very strange. Who is in charge? It's never out right stated. Compare this to the Elder Scrolls series, where you have the Empire, the Aldmeri, etc.

This is a one and done game for me. The game feels like they just gave up after Fort Joy when it comes to character interaction and becomes a series of set pieces. I cared less about the world as the game went on and nothing of importance actually happened. 

Tutorial Area 10/10
Fort Joy 10/10
Ripper Coast 6/10
Nameless Isle 4/10
Arx 4/10
Final Battle 3/10
The "epilogue" sucks. Buy this game on a discount.

review:
This game has become a bit of an obsession of mine, for good reason! I love the combat, especially playing with surfaces. 

I'm glad I own both Divinity: Original Sin 1 and 2, because they're similar enough to tickle my strategy-brain in an exquisite way, but also different enough that I can play one or the other depending on my mood. This one is great if you want to struggle and triumph your way through a fantasy world that often feels harsh, but has glimmers of hope. It pushes you down just enough to make it feel fantastic when you fight to break free and make things better. This game also has a deeper story than its predecessor, with more fleshed-out characters, moral grayness, and impactful choices. 

I'm still not completely sure whether I prefer the combat mechanics more between Original Sin 1 or 2, but that's all the more reason to keep playing both!
